title: Once-weekly semaglutide in people with HIV-associated lipohypertrophy: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase IIb single-centred clinical trial

what_it_measured.text: The primary aim of this trial was to investigate effects of the glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist, semaglutide, on AT in HIV-associated lipohypertrophy.
We investigated the effects of semaglutide on the quantity and distribution of adipose tissue among PWH and HIV-associated lipohypertrophy.

dose.text: The titration phase, designed to minimize initial drug side effects for those randomised to receive semaglutide, consisted of weekly 0·25 mg SC semaglutide injections for 4 weeks, followed by weekly 0·5 mg SC semaglutide injections for another
After the titration phase, participants received 1·0 mg SC semaglutide weekly for 24 weeks or matching placebo.

route.text: Participants were randomised 1:1 to receive 32 weeks of once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide (8-week dose titration+24 weeks at 1·0 mg) or placebo; all personnel/ participants remained masked to treatment assignment.
Estimated effect sizes of semaglutide on outcome measures in people with HIV-associated lipohypertrophy treated with 32 weeks of once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide or matching placebo βa
Adverse events in people with HIV-associated lipohypertrophy treated with 32 weeks of once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide or matching placebo Semaglutide (n=54)

endpoint.text: Significant effects of semaglutide were seen over the 32-week study period in sex-adjusted multiplicative regression analyses for the primary outcome of interest, abdominal visceral AT [β (95% CI); estimated % change: −30·82 cm2 (−50·13, −11·51); −30·6%].
Primary outcomes included changes at 32 weeks in AT quantity by body compartment.

In the final GEE multiplicative regression models, semaglutide showed statistically significant effects at 32 weeks for all primary outcomes and anthropometric measurements except pericardial fat (table 2).

reported_results.text: There were no statistically significant differences in possibly-related/related adverse events [absolute risk difference (95% CI): 0·1111 (−0·0727, 0·2869); however, one semaglutide-related grade 4 elevated lipase and two possibly-related cases of cholelithiasis (grades 1 and 2) were observed.

Significant effects of semaglutide were seen over the 32-week study period in sex-adjusted multiplicative regression analyses for the primary outcome of interest, abdominal visceral AT [β (95% CI); estimated % change: −30·82 cm2 (−50·13, −11·51); −30·6%].
Findings—Between June 10, 2019 to July 28, 2022, 108 participants were randomised to receive semaglutide (n=54) or placebo (n=54).

A greater number (%) of participants within the semaglutide group demonstrated a loss of >5% body weight [30 (65·2%) vs. 2 (4·4%)] with odds ratio of 41·3 (95% CI [8·8, 192·7]; p<0·0001). 39 (84·8%) and 30 (65·2%) participants within the semaglutide group lost >5% TBF and abdominal VAT area, respectively; however, no variable was predictive of these >5% losses (all p>0·10: baseline BMI, HbA1c%, and CD4+ T-cell count; current TAF or INSTI use; age, sex, ART duration).
Pericardial fat had an estimated 16·5% reduction but did not reach statistical significance.
Effects of semaglutide were not statistically significant for LBM or psoas muscle volume (i.e., muscle mass); however, both showed estimated decreases of 5·7% and 5·3%, respectively.
